item.title: Choosing a mesh resolution
item.content:
Before you texture the Airline Chair, you need to decide how many polygons it will have, because the texture is laid out on the polygons themselves. In this short part you'll see why that decision comes first, and how to apply the Subdivision Surface modifier at the level you want to work with. You'll need the chair you modeled in the Modeling the Airline Chair series. The video uses Blender 2.83.

Decide what the model is for

  1. Think about where it will be used. 0:00 A low-polygon mesh, with only a few polygons, suits a game engine or real-time rendering such as VR or AR. A really polished, high-quality render, like one in an advertisement or a film, can use far more. Which one you're making changes your texturing workflow.

  2. Compare the two versions. 0:36 The video keeps the original model in one collection (original base meshes) and a high-resolution version of the same model in another. Each piece of the original still has its Subdivision Surface modifier, set to 3 in the viewport.

Why the resolution comes first

  1. Apply the modifier to make it real geometry. 0:46 To make the high-resolution version, select a piece of the original, and in its Subdivision Surface modifier click Apply. The video applied it with Viewport set to 3; lower it to 1 before you click Apply and you get a much more reasonable polygonal mesh 1:14.

  2. Don't smooth after texturing. 1:28 The video undoes the change to explain. The texture is assigned to the shape of the polygons. If you texture the low-polygon shape and then smooth it, there are suddenly more edges, so Blender doesn't know which edge a seam belongs to: a seam you set on one edge may end up somewhere else. To avoid that, decide which resolution you're working with from the start 2:08.

Choose a level

  1. New to this? Use the base mesh or one level. 2:13 If you're not yet confident working with a lot of polygons, work with the base mesh, or apply just one level of subdivision: set Viewport to 1 and click Apply.

  2. Shade it smooth and check it. 2:30 Select the piece, right-click and choose Shade Smooth, then turn off the wireframe. That's halfway decent: it will give you a pretty good render with really minimal geometry.

  3. For a polished render, apply level 3. 2:55 If you want a really polished render and smooth geometry, apply the modifier with Viewport set to 3. From then on you're working with all of those polygons, so you need more advanced skills in selecting polygons, edge loops and so on 3:05. It's not that hard, but if you're just getting into this it may hold you up.

Wrap-up

A texture follows the polygons it's laid out on, so choose the chair's resolution before you texture it: the base mesh or one level of subdivision if you're new to this, three levels for a polished render. Apply the Subdivision Surface modifier at that level, and keep working with that mesh from then on.
